screens.prompt: In D9, count the North orders that are still open with one function taking two conditions.

hints.syntax: =COUNTIFS(B2:B8,"North",C2:C8,"Open"): pairs of range and condition, all true at once.
hints.func-countifs: COUNTIF takes one condition. A second condition needs COUNTIFS.
hints.require-ref: Point the first range at the region column and the second at the status column.
hints.value: Rows 2, 6 and 8 are North and open. Row 4 is North but closed, so it does not count.
hints.error: Ranges of different heights leave #VALUE! on the sheet. Check that both cover rows 2 to 8.

reject.why: one condition only, so the closed North order is counted too and the answer is 4
a COUNTIFS with no second pair is a COUNTIF wearing the wrong name
the opposite status, so only row 3 counts and the answer is 1
the ranges start on row 3, so row 2 drops out of the count
division by zero, so the cell holds #DIV/0!
the missing comma jams a range and a condition into one argument
the right number 3, but this lesson is a COUNTIFS exercise

screens.prompt: In D9, count the open orders that came to more than 5 units.

hints.syntax: =COUNTIFS(C2:C8,"Open",D2:D8,">5"): the comparison sits inside the quotes.
hints.func-countifs: Two conditions over one table is what COUNTIFS is built for.
hints.require-ref: Compare the threshold against the units column, so >5 is tested on real cells.
hints.value: Rows 6 and 8 are open with 6 and 8 units. Row 2 has exactly 5, so it does not count.
hints.error: A missing comma jams the two pairs into one argument, and Excel refuses the formula.

reject.why: one condition only, so the closed 8-unit order is counted too and the answer is 3
at least 5 pulls in row 2 as well, which is 5 units and not more
the wrong status, so only the closed 8-unit order counts and the answer is 1
the ranges start on row 3, so the first order is never counted
division by zero, so the cell holds #DIV/0!

docs.explain:
COUNTIFS counts the rows where every condition holds at the same time. Its arguments alternate range, condition, range, condition, and each range has to cover the same rows. COUNTIF does the same job for a single condition, which is why a second pair needs the other function.

Here B2:B8 must read North and C2:C8 must read Open, so rows 2, 6 and 8 qualify and the answer is 3. Asking COUNTIF for North alone returns 4, and the extra row is the closed North order in row 4.

The second screen swaps one text condition for a comparison, so D2:D8 has to come to more than 5 units. Row 2 holds exactly 5 and drops out, leaving 2. Comparisons travel inside quotes, and every condition you add can only narrow the count.

errors.text: One criteria range covers a different number of rows from the others, so the conditions stop lining up.
Two conditions that exclude each other, such as North and South on the same column, can never both hold for one row, and the count comes back as 0.
Dropping the second pair counts every North order, which is 4 rather than 3.

seo.title: COUNTIFS in Excel: several conditions
seo.description: COUNTIF counts cells that match one condition, COUNTIFS counts rows where two conditions hold. Each extra range must match in size, or the count drifts.
